274.title: Hillel on the roof (Yoma 35b)
274.hook: too poor for the fee, young Hillel lay on the skylight in the snow to hear the lesson
274.howItsDone: Jewish tradition treats Torah study as open to everyone, rich or poor, and the story of Hillel on the roof is often told to children and adults to show how much learning is worth.

segments.voice: Yesterday Shammai pushed a questioner away with a builder's rod. Your line was be patient like Hillel. Did someone test your patience? Today, how Hillel himself learned. Day two hundred seventy-four.

Think of the last time you really wanted to be somewhere and couldn't afford it. A concert. A class. A trip your friends were taking. You stood outside it, in a way. Before Hillel was the great Hillel, he was a poor young man from Babylonia, working for tiny wages in Jerusalem. The best teachers in the city taught in a study house with a guard at the door and a fee to get in. One winter day he didn't have the fee. Today, what he did instead.
screen: `OUTSIDE SOMETHING YOU WANTED.` → `A POOR YOUNG MAN IN JERUSALEM.` → `NO FEE TODAY.`

segments.voice: The story is in the Talmud, tractate Yoma. Every day Hillel worked and earned a small coin. Half he gave to the guard of the study house, where the teachers Shemaya and Avtalyon taught. Half fed his family. One day he earned nothing, and the guard wouldn't let him in. So Hillel climbed up onto the roof, and lay down by the skylight, so he could hear the words of the living God from their mouths. It was a Friday in the dead of winter, and snow began to fall. He stayed. The snow covered him. In the morning, Shemaya said to Avtalyon: my brother, every day this house is bright, and today it's dark. Is it cloudy? They looked up and saw the shape of a man in the skylight. They climbed up and found Hillel under a thick layer of snow. They brought him down, washed him, rubbed him with oil, and sat him by the fire, though it was Shabbat. And they said: this one is worth breaking the Sabbath for. Saving a life overrides Shabbat for anyone; the line is their way of saying how much they loved him. The Talmud tells the story for a reason. It says that when poor people are asked why they didn't learn, the answer comes back: were you poorer than Hillel? That's a hard question. But it isn't a scolding. It's an invitation. Learning finds a way in, even through the roof.
screen: `HALF FOR THE GUARD, HALF FOR HOME.` · `ONTO THE ROOF, BY THE SKYLIGHT.` · `THE HOUSE IS DARK TODAY.` · `WERE YOU POORER THAN HILLEL?` · then, large: `LISTEN THROUGH THE SNOW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find your skylight. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you want to learn and keep putting off. A language. An instrument. A text. How to fix the thing that keeps breaking. What's your guard at the door? Time, money, feeling too old, feeling behind? Now picture the skylight: one small way in anyway. A free library book. Ten minutes before bed. A question to someone who knows. Hold that one way in. The bell holds the time.
Hillel on the roof. Too poor to pay, he lay on the skylight in the snow to hear the lesson, and his teachers said he was worth breaking Shabbat for.
Your line: listen through the snow. Today, go a little out of your way to learn one thing, even if you have to find a skylight. Day two hundred seventy-four.

275.title: Water wears stone (Avot de-Rabbi Natan 6)
275.hook: Akiva, an unlettered shepherd of forty, sees water carve a hole in rock
275.howItsDone: Akiva's stone is one of the most retold stories in Jewish education, used to encourage adult beginners; many Jews study a little every day, drop by drop.

segments.voice: Yesterday young Hillel lay in the snow on the roof to hear a lesson. Your line was listen through the snow. Did you find a skylight? Day two hundred seventy-five.

Maybe you've said it. I'm too old to start that now. Too old to learn piano, to go back to school, to read the book everyone else read in college. Picture a man of forty, a shepherd, who by the story's telling can't read a single letter. Not one. He's standing by a well, and he notices a stone with a hole worn right through it. That man is going to become Rabbi Akiva, one of the greatest teachers the Jewish people ever had. And it starts with that stone.
screen: `TOO OLD TO START.` → `A SHEPHERD OF FORTY.` → `A STONE WITH A HOLE IN IT.`

segments.voice: The story is in Avot de-Rabbi Natan, an early companion to Pirkei Avot. Akiva is forty and has learned nothing. At a well he sees a stone hollowed out, and asks: who carved this? They tell him: the water that falls on it, every day, all the time. And they quote Job: "The waters wear the stones." Akiva stands there and reasons it out. If something soft like water can carve something hard like stone, then the words of Torah, which are strong as iron, can surely carve a way into my heart, which is only flesh and blood. So he goes to school. A grown man, with his little son, sitting with the children's teacher. He takes one end of the writing tablet, his son takes the other, and they learn the alphabet together. Alef, bet. Then the first book of the Torah. Then the rest. The story says that within years he was teaching crowds. The water isn't a flood. It's drops. Nothing happens on the first day, or the hundredth. The stone looks exactly the same for a very long time. Then one day there's a hole. That's the picture Akiva carried: not talent, not a lightning bolt, but a small thing done every day for a long time. It's also why this path gives you one small lesson a day.
screen: `WHO CARVED THIS STONE?` · `SOFT WATER, HARD STONE.` · `A MAN OF FORTY LEARNS ALEF-BET.` · `DROPS, NOT A FLOOD.` · then, large: `WATER WEARS STONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pick your stone. Settle, and breathe. Think of one hard habit you'd like to change or build. Something that hasn't budged when you tried to move it all at once. Now shrink it to a drop: the smallest version you could do every single day. One page. One push-up. One kind text. One minute of quiet. Picture doing that drop tomorrow, and the day after, and a year of days. Let the stone wait. The bell holds the time.
Water wears stone. Akiva, at forty, saw water carve a rock and reasoned: if water can do that, words of Torah can carve my heart.
Your line: water wears stone. Today, do the smallest drop of your hard habit, and plan to do it again tomorrow. Day two hundred seventy-five.

276.title: Akiva and Rachel (Ketubot 62b–63a)
276.hook: his wife sends him to study for years; he tells his students that all they have is hers
276.howItsDone: The story of Akiva and Rachel is told at weddings and in classes as a picture of a partnership built on learning; many Jewish scholars today still thank their spouses publicly when they finish a work.

segments.voice: Yesterday Akiva saw a stone worn through by drops. Your line was water wears stone. Did you do your one small drop? Today, the person who made his drops possible. Day two hundred seventy-six.

Watch the end of any awards show. Someone holds up a statue and thanks their spouse, their mom, the teacher who stayed late. Sometimes it's a line. Sometimes you can tell the person in the audience gave up years for this. Behind almost every big story there's somebody who isn't on stage. The Talmud tells Rabbi Akiva's story twice: once as the man and the stone, and once as the woman who believed in him before anyone else did. Today, her.
screen: `THE ACCEPTANCE SPEECH.` → `SOMEONE NOT ON STAGE.` → `THE WOMAN BEHIND AKIVA.`

segments.voice: In tractate Ketubot, Akiva is a shepherd working for Kalba Savua, one of the richest men in Jerusalem. The rich man's daughter sees something in him: that he's modest and good. She tells him: if I marry you, will you go and study? He says yes. They marry quietly, and her father, furious, cuts her off without a penny. Tradition knows her as Rachel. Akiva goes away to study for twelve years. When he comes home, he hears an old man mocking her outside the house: how long will you live like a widow with a living husband? And she answers: if he listened to me, he'd stay away another twelve. So he turns around, without even going in, and studies twelve more. When he finally returns, twenty-four thousand students walk with him. His wife goes out to meet him, and falls at his feet. The students don't know who she is, and start to push her away. Akiva stops them. Leave her, he says. What is mine and what is yours is hers. Everything I know, and everything I've taught you, belongs to her. There are parts of this story that are hard to hear today: years apart, poverty, a father's anger. The Talmud doesn't hide them. But its last word is gratitude, said out loud, in front of everyone.
screen: `THE RICH MAN'S DAUGHTER.` · `WILL YOU GO AND STUDY?` · `TWELVE YEARS, THEN TWELVE MORE.` · `LEAVE HER. SHE'S THE REASON.` · then, large: `WHAT IS MINE IS HERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the person behind your work. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you're proud of. A skill, a job, a child you've raised, a hard year you got through. Now look behind it. Who made room for it? Who covered for you, drove you, fed you, believed in you before there was any reason to? Let one face come. Stay with them. What would you say if you had the microphone? The bell holds the time.
Akiva and Rachel. She sent him to study for years, and when he came back with thousands of students, he said: what is mine and yours is hers.
Your line: what is mine is hers. Today, tell one person behind your work, out loud or in writing, that part of it is theirs. Day two hundred seventy-six.

277.title: Honi draws a circle (Taanit 23a)
277.hook: in drought, Honi draws a circle and won't step out until it rains
277.howItsDone: Jewish prayer includes asking for rain in its season; from late fall until Passover a line for rain is added to the daily Amidah, and stories like Honi's are told about bold, personal prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday Akiva told his students everything was his wife's. Your line was what is mine is hers. Did you thank someone behind your work? Day two hundred seventy-seven.

Most of us are polite when we ask for things. If it's not too much trouble. Only if you have time. Totally fine if not. We shrink our requests so no one has to say no. Now picture a dry land in late winter. The rains haven't come. Fields are cracking, cisterns are empty, and the people go to one man, known for his prayers, and say: pray for rain. He does. Nothing happens. So he picks up a stick and draws a circle in the dirt around himself. Today, Honi, and a prayer that was anything but polite.
screen: `ONLY IF IT'S NO TROUBLE.` → `A LAND WITHOUT RAIN.` → `A CIRCLE IN THE DIRT.`

segments.voice: The story is in the Mishnah and the Talmud, tractate Taanit. Honi stands inside his circle and speaks to God. Master of the world, your children have turned to me, because I'm like a member of your household. I swear by your great name, I won't move from this circle until you have mercy on your children. A few drops fall. Honi says: that's not what I asked for. I asked for rain to fill the cisterns and the pits and the caves. Now it pours, violent and frightening. Honi says: not that either. I asked for rain of goodwill, of blessing, of generosity. And then it rains the right way, steadily, until the people have to climb the Temple Mount to get out of the water. Now they ask him to pray for it to stop. That's how he got his name: Honi the circle-drawer. The great sage of the time, Shimon ben Shetach, sent him a message that is half scolding and half wonder. If you weren't Honi, I'd put you under a ban. But what can I do? You nag God like a child nagging his father, and his father gives him what he wants. That's the heart of it. Honi isn't bargaining like a stranger. He's asking like family, boldly and specifically, and not taking drizzle for an answer.
screen: `I WON'T STEP OUT OF THIS CIRCLE.` · `NOT DRIZZLE. NOT A FLOOD.` · `RAIN OF BLESSING.` · `LIKE A CHILD WITH A PARENT.` · then, large: `DRAW THE CIRCLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: draw your circle. Settle, and breathe. Picture a circle drawn around where you sit. Inside it, name one thing you really want, for yourself or for someone else. Not the polite version. The real one, specific: not things getting better, but this person healing, this debt paid, this friendship mended. If you pray, you can ask for it the way Honi did, like family. If not, simply say it clearly inside yourself and stay in the circle with it. The bell holds the time.
Honi draws a circle. In a drought he drew a circle, refused to step out until rain came, and then asked for the right rain.
Your line: draw the circle. Today, ask for one thing clearly and specifically, without shrinking it first. Day two hundred seventy-seven.

278.title: The carob tree (Taanit 23a)
278.hook: an old man plants a tree he'll never eat from, for his grandchildren
278.howItsDone: The carob story is often told on Tu BiShvat, the new year of trees, when many Jews plant trees or eat fruit such as carob, and it is a favorite teaching about caring for future generations.

segments.voice: Yesterday Honi drew a circle and wouldn't step out until the rain came. Your line was draw the circle. Did you ask for something without shrinking it? Day two hundred seventy-eight.

Somebody planted the big tree on your street. Somebody laid the stones of the oldest building in your town, dug the well, started the library, wrote down the recipe your family still makes. Most of them never saw you. They never knew your name. They just did the work and left it for whoever came next. The Talmud tells a story about Honi, the circle-drawer, walking down a road and meeting one of those people. An old man, on his knees, planting a tree.
screen: `WHO PLANTED YOUR STREET'S TREE?` → `THEY NEVER KNEW YOUR NAME.` → `AN OLD MAN, PLANTING.`

segments.voice: It's the same page of tractate Taanit as yesterday's circle. Honi sees a man planting a carob tree. Carob is slow; it takes years before it bears fruit. Honi asks him: how long until this tree gives fruit? The man says: seventy years. Honi presses him. Are you so sure you'll live another seventy years? And the man gives an answer people have been repeating ever since. I found this world full of carob trees. Just as my ancestors planted for me, I'm planting for my children. That's it. No speech about legacy. Just a debt noticed and paid forward. Everything he eats, he says, somebody planted before him. So he plants too, knowing someone else will eat. Seventy years matters in this story. In the Bible, seventy years is a whole human life. The man is planting past the edge of his own life, on purpose. The story keeps going from here, and Honi's next seventy years will surprise him. We'll come back to that. For today, stay with the old man in the dirt. It's a small picture of how a tradition works at all. Every teaching you've heard on this path, somebody planted. They memorized it, copied it, argued over it, carried it through exile, and passed it down to people they'd never meet. Including you.
screen: `HOW LONG UNTIL IT BEARS FRUIT?` · `SEVENTY YEARS.` · `MY ANCESTORS PLANTED FOR ME.` · `A TRADITION IS PLANTED TOO.` · then, large: `PLANT FOR OTHERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find your carob trees, then plant one. Settle, and breathe. Look around wherever you are. Name three things in reach that someone made or planted before you ever arrived. A chair, a road, a word you use. Say thank you, silently, to people you'll never meet. Now think of one small thing you could start today that someone else will enjoy after you. A seed in a pot. A note in a book. Teaching a kid a family recipe. The bell holds the time.
The carob tree. An old man plants one that won't bear fruit for seventy years, because his ancestors planted for him.
Your line: plant for others. Today, start one small thing that someone after you will get to enjoy. Day two hundred seventy-eight.

279.title: This too is for good (Taanit 21a)
279.hook: Nachum of Gamzu met every setback by saying this too is for good
279.howItsDone: Gam zu l'tovah is an everyday Jewish expression, said when plans fall through; a related saying in the Talmud, attributed to Rabbi Akiva, is that everything the Merciful One does is for good.

segments.voice: Yesterday an old man planted a carob tree for his grandchildren. Your line was plant for others. Did you start something for someone after you? Day two hundred seventy-nine.

You miss the train. The coffee spills. The email you were waiting for says no. There's a split second before you react where you get to decide what this is. A disaster? An annoyance? A story you'll tell later? One sage in the Talmud was famous for filling that split second with the same three Hebrew words, every single time. Gam zu l'tovah. This too is for good. People called him Nachum Ish Gam Zu. Nachum, the this-too man. Today, his story, and what those words do and don't mean.
screen: `THE TRAIN, THE COFFEE, THE NO.` → `A SPLIT SECOND TO DECIDE.` → `NACHUM, THE THIS-TOO MAN.`

segments.voice: Tractate Taanit tells this. The Jewish community wanted to send a gift to the emperor in Rome, and chose Nachum to carry it, because miracles seemed to follow him. They gave him a chest full of jewels. On the way he stopped at an inn. In the night, the innkeepers opened the chest, stole the jewels, and filled it with dirt. In the morning Nachum saw what had happened. And he said: this too is for good. He arrived at the palace and opened the chest before the emperor. Dirt. The emperor was furious and ordered him killed. Then the story turns. A stranger appeared among the emperor's advisers; the Talmud says it was the prophet Elijah. He said: maybe this is the dirt of their ancestor Abraham, who threw dust that turned into swords. The Romans tried it in a battle they were losing, and it worked. Nachum went home honored, his chest full of treasure. Now, a careful point. The same passage says Nachum lived with great suffering: he was blind, with no hands or feet, and his body was covered in sores. So his three words weren't a smile pasted over pain. They were a way of trusting that the story isn't finished yet. Nachum doesn't say this is good. He says this, too, is for good. The word for is doing a lot of work.
screen: `A CHEST OF JEWELS FOR ROME.` · `STOLEN, FILLED WITH DIRT.` · `THE DIRT BECOMES A WEAPON.` · `NOT GOOD: FOR GOOD.` · then, large: `GAM ZU L'TOVAH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: try the three words on a small thing. Settle, and breathe. Pick one annoyance from this week. Not a tragedy; something small. The delayed package. The canceled plan. Picture it clearly, and notice the story you told yourself about it. Now try Nachum's words: gam zu l'tovah, this too is for good. You don't have to know how. Just leave the ending open. Notice if anything loosens. The bell holds the time.
Gam zu l'tovah. Hebrew for this too is for good. Nachum of Gamzu said it at every setback, trusting the story wasn't over.
Your line: this too for the good. Today, when one small thing goes wrong, say the three words and leave the ending open. Day two hundred seventy-nine.

280.title: It is not in heaven (Bava Metzia 59b)
280.hook: a heavenly voice backs Rabbi Eliezer, and the sages answer: the Torah is not in heaven (Deuteronomy 30:12)
280.howItsDone: Jewish law is decided by reasoned argument among scholars, following rules such as the majority view, and the story of the oven of Akhnai is one of the best-known texts used to teach this.

segments.voice: Yesterday Nachum met every setback with gam zu l'tovah. Your line was this too for the good. Did you leave an ending open? Day two hundred eighty.

Imagine you're in the middle of an argument, and the other person says: if I'm right, let that tree prove it. And the tree pulls itself out of the ground and moves a hundred cubits. You'd probably lose the argument right there. In the Talmud, it didn't work. The rabbis were debating a small legal question about whether a certain kind of clay oven could become ritually impure. Rabbi Eliezer said one thing. Everyone else said another. And what happened next is one of the most famous pages in the Talmud.
screen: `IF I'M RIGHT, LET THE TREE PROVE IT.` → `A QUESTION ABOUT AN OVEN.` → `ONE AGAINST ALL.`

segments.voice: In tractate Bava Metzia, Rabbi Eliezer brings every argument in the world, and the sages don't accept them. So he says: if the law is as I say, let this carob tree prove it. The tree uproots itself. The sages answer: you don't bring proof from a carob tree. Let the stream prove it. The water flows backward. You don't bring proof from a stream. Let the walls of the study house prove it. The walls begin to lean. Rabbi Yehoshua scolds the walls: when scholars argue, what business is it of yours? So they don't fall, out of respect for Rabbi Yehoshua, and they don't straighten, out of respect for Rabbi Eliezer. The Talmud says they're still leaning. Finally a voice comes from heaven: why do you argue with Rabbi Eliezer? The law is like him everywhere. And Rabbi Yehoshua stands up and quotes the Torah: "It is not in heaven." Those words come from Deuteronomy, where Moses tells the people the teaching isn't far away or up in the sky; it's close, in your mouth and in your heart. Another sage explains: the Torah was already given at Sinai. We don't decide law by voices from heaven. The Torah itself says to follow the majority. That's a startling move. The sages take the Torah so seriously that they refuse a miracle. Once the teaching is given, it's in human hands, to be argued, reasoned, and decided here on earth.
screen: `THE TREE, THE STREAM, THE WALLS.` · `A VOICE FROM HEAVEN.` · `IT IS NOT IN HEAVEN.` · `NOW IT'S IN HUMAN HANDS.` · then, large: `IT IS NOT IN HEAVEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, and a look back at this week. Hillel on the roof, water wearing stone, Akiva and Rachel, Honi's circle, the carob tree, gam zu l'tovah. Now settle, and breathe. Pick one question you've been waiting for someone else to answer for you. A decision, a belief, a hard choice. Instead of waiting for a sign, think it through for yourself for one minute. What do you know? What would a wise friend say? What's close, in your own mouth and heart? The bell holds the time.
It is not in heaven. Words from Deuteronomy that the sages used to refuse a heavenly voice: the Torah was given, and now it's ours to reason through.
screen: `IT IS NOT IN HEAVEN — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: it is not in heaven. Today, take one question you've been waiting on, and think it through yourself. Day two hundred eighty.

trapdoor: what you thought: a miracle story.
what it means: the rabbis refuse a miracle, because the Torah is now in human hands.
what a scholar hears: the argument is about the oven of Akhnai, and Rabbi Yirmiyah grounds the majority rule in a reading of Exodus 23:2.
